justification_text:
The point estimates at each time horizon were driven by an expectation of stability or equilibrium in the variable being forecasted, likely informed by recent trends or historical data. In this case, it appears that the value of 198.51 was chosen as the most likely outcome, reflecting a central tendency or mean based on prior information. Over the different time horizons (1 day, 1 week, and 1 month), the point estimate remained constant because no anticipated changes—such as a shift in trend or external shock—were deemed significant enough to adjust the central value in the near term. Essentially, the forecast assumes that the factors affecting this variable will not materially change in the time periods assessed, so shorter- and longer-term predictions anchor around the same baseline.

The confidence intervals widen as the forecast horizon extends, reflecting growing uncertainty over time. On a 1-day horizon, many of the inputs influencing the outcome are more predictable, and unexpected deviations are less likely, leading to a tighter range of uncertainty. At the 1-week mark, however, there is more time for random fluctuations, potential news, or external factors to cause variation, so the range becomes broader. By the 1-month horizon, the width of the confidence interval is even larger because the accumulation of uncertainties—whether due to market volatility, external events, or unknown variables—becomes more pronounced. Essentially, the factors influencing this variable become harder to predict the further out in time the projection extends.

There are, of course, specific risks or events that could lead to outcomes outside the stated confidence intervals. For example, if this forecast pertains to a stock price, a major earnings announcement, regulatory changes, or macroeconomic shocks could significantly impact the value in ways not accounted for in the underlying data or assumptions. For longer horizons like 1 month, such risks grow because there is more time for these rare or unpredictable events to unfold. The confidence intervals aim to capture a high probability of outcomes (90%), but extreme scenarios—such as geopolitical crises, supply chain disruptions, or unexpected economic indicators—fall outside the modeled uncertainty and could push the outcome beyond even the widest interval.
